title: Always joyful
hook: Rebbe Nachman taught that being joyful always is a great mitzvah

segments.voice: Yesterday, two souls, two kings and one small city. Your line was two souls. At one decision, did you hear both voices before you chose? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

A wedding, late at night. The music is loud and a circle of dancers is spinning. Off to the side stands a man who isn't dancing. His face is heavy. Something is wrong in his life, and it shows. Then two of the dancers break the circle, take him by the hands, and pull him in. He resists for a step or two. Then he's turning with them, still carrying whatever he carries, but carried along too. Rebbe Nachman of Breslov used a scene like this to teach about joy. And he made a demand about it that sounds impossible. Today's words are the demand.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF DANCERS.` → `A MAN WITH A HEAVY FACE.` → `PULLED INTO THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman taught that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always. First, the word always. In Hebrew it's tamid, the word for the offering that was brought in the Temple without a break, morning and evening. The psalm uses it too: "I have set the LORD always before me." Always isn't a mood. It's a practice that keeps going. Second, it's work. Rebbe Nachman didn't pretend joy comes easily. Breslov teaching passes on his advice that a person should push with all their strength to be glad, and when nothing else works, to do something a little silly, something light, to break the heaviness. Joy, here, is something you make, not something you wait for. Third, the circle. That's the scene from the hook, and it's his. When joy is strong, it doesn't run from sadness. It reaches over, takes sadness by the hands, and pulls it into the dance. The sadness isn't erased. It's brought in, and it starts to move. Fourth, how this differs from a week ago. Simcha, we said, opens the heart. Rebbe Nachman adds the hard part: always. On the bad days too. Especially then. Not because pain doesn't matter, but because, for him, a heavy heart is the very place joy is needed most.
screen: `TAMID: WITHOUT A BREAK.` · `JOY IS WORK, NOT WEATHER.` · `JOY PULLS SADNESS INTO THE DANCE.` · `ON THE BAD DAYS TOO.` · then, large: `ALWAYS JOYFUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be joyful for one minute, on purpose. Settle, and breathe. You don't need a reason. Let the corners of your mouth lift, even if it feels a little silly. Rebbe Nachman wouldn't mind silly. Breathe in, and think of one thing you're glad exists. Breathe out, and let a little of the heaviness go. If something hard is sitting with you today, don't push it away. Invite it into the circle: you can come too. If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words, I have set the LORD always before me. The bell holds the time.
Always joyful. Rebbe Nachman's teaching that being joyful always is a great mitzvah: joy as steady work, pulling sadness into the dance. Today's words.
Your line: always joyful. Today, at the heaviest moment, do one small light thing on purpose: hum, stretch, smile at nothing. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim sing and dance as a deliberate practice of joy, and the saying that it is a great mitzvah to be joyful always has been set to song.

original.note: Hebrew: always, continually. Also the name of the daily Temple offering.

trapdoor: what you thought: be happy all the time, no matter what.
what it means: joy as a steady practice, kept up on purpose, even on the heavy days, reaching for sadness instead of running from it.
what a scholar hears: Likutei Moharan's 'mitzvah gedolah lihyot b'simchah tamid', with tamid echoing the Temple's continual offering.

notes: Psalm 16:8 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm.
Likutei Moharan II:24 paraphrased (great mitzvah to be joyful always; strive with all strength; use silliness if needed). Please confirm that the 'silliness' advice is in II:24.
The dance-circle image (joy grabbing sadness and pulling it into the dance) is paraphrased from Likutei Moharan II:23; please confirm the source.
Tamid as the name of the continual offering (Numbers 28:3–4, 'olat tamid'); confirm.
'He knew sadness from the inside' rests on Breslov tradition about Rebbe Nachman's struggles; confirm or soften.
howItsDone says the saying 'is often set to song'; confirm.
Editor pass: dropped 'Turn it four ways'; cut the biographical claim 'he knew sadness from the inside' (teach and myth), which Likutei Moharan II:24 does not state; softened 'often set to song'.
